planting.note: Transplant seedlings into flooded paddy soil once it is reliably warm; this is a tall, photoperiod-sensitive autumn landrace grown as a single annual crop, so plan for a long season rather than a quick turnaround.

directions: Tám Xoan Hải Hậu is a tall-strawed, photoperiod-sensitive aromatic japonica landrace grown in the coastal alluvial soils of Hải Hậu district, Nam Định province, in Vietnam's Red River Delta, where it has been cultivated and selected for roughly two centuries and historically served as tribute rice for the imperial court. It is raised as a single long-duration autumn crop, with seedlings started in a flooded nursery bed and transplanted into puddled paddy soil, then grown under shallow standing water through most of the vegetative period before the field is drained ahead of a November harvest. The plant produces sparse, slender panicles bearing small, long, ivory-white grains with an intense natural fragrance that holds up well after milling and cooking. Because of its narrow local adaptation and long growth cycle, it is best approached as a specialty single-season planting rather than grown for repeated harvests.

planting.note: Transplant into flooded, slightly acidic alluvial paddy soil; this is a tall, lodging-prone, photoperiod-sensitive landrace grown as a single long-season annual crop rather than a quick-turnaround planting.

directions: Named for the market at Chợ Đào in Mỹ Lệ commune, Cần Đước district, Long An province, this fragrant landrace can only be reliably grown true-to-type within a small cluster of local hamlets on alluvial, slightly acid-sulfate soil, and was historically sent as tribute rice to the Nguyễn court. The grains are small, long, and unusually tall-strawed for a Vietnamese rice, each kernel containing a small pinkish inner spot locally called 'hạt lựu' (pomegranate seed), and the milled rice keeps a strong aroma for months when stored properly. Start seedlings in a flooded nursery bed and transplant into puddled paddy soil, maintaining shallow standing water through the long vegetative period and providing support or wider spacing to offset its tendency to lodge. Because it is grown as a single annual crop over roughly six months, it does not suit the multiple short cycles used for high-yield modern varieties.

planting.note: Direct-seed or transplant into flooded paddy once soil is consistently warm; this short-duration semi-dwarf type can be grown twice a year in a warm climate, unlike older long-season landraces.

directions: ST25, short for 'Sóc Trăng 25,' is a semi-dwarf, short-duration jasmine-type rice developed over roughly two decades by breeder Hồ Quang Cua and colleagues in Sóc Trăng province in the Mekong Delta, and it has repeatedly been judged the world's best rice at international rice-trade competitions beginning in 2019. The grains are long and non-chalky, cooking up soft and faintly sweet with a natural pandan-like fragrance, while the sturdy, lodging-resistant stem and tolerance of soil salinity and major leaf diseases make it well suited to the brackish lower Mekong Delta. Direct-seed or transplant into flooded paddy soil kept consistently warm and wet through tillering, then drain before harvest; its short growth cycle allows two crops per year rather than the single long season required by traditional photoperiod-sensitive landraces.

common_name: Khao Kai Noi Rice (Lao Glutinous Landrace)

planting.note: Transplant from a flooded nursery bed into puddled rainfed-lowland paddy soil after monsoon rains establish; this is a late-maturing single annual crop, not suited to a short-season planting.

directions: Khao Kai Noi, meaning roughly 'small chicken rice,' is a glutinous rainfed-lowland landrace first documented in Houaphanh province in northeastern Laos and now also widely grown in neighboring Xieng Khouang province. Farmers maintain at least nine recognized color and habit variants, distinguished mainly by glume color (yellow, red, black, white, or striped) and by upland versus lowland adaptation, the product of generations of on-farm selection rather than formal breeding, and the variety is listed in the Slow Food Ark of Taste as a landrace at risk of displacement by higher-yielding modern glutinous types. Its small, rounded grains are notably shatter-resistant and difficult to thresh, and once steamed they cook up soft, sticky, and aromatic, traditionally used for sticky rice, rice noodles, rice cakes, and fermented rice beverages. Start seedlings in a flooded nursery bed and transplant into puddled paddy after the monsoon rains begin, keeping shallow standing water through the long vegetative period typical of this late-maturing single-crop variety.

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring in a humid, frost-free tropical climate; Ri6 needs the same sustained warmth above 50F as other durian cultivars and is realistically limited to the most tropical microclimates or greenhouse culture outside true tropical zones.

directions: Ri6 originated in Long Hồ district, Vĩnh Long province, in Vietnam's Mekong Delta, where it was selected and propagated from a local seedling tree in the 1990s by a grower known locally as 'Sáu Ri,' from whom the cultivar takes its name. It bears large, rounded fruit, commonly 3 to 5 kilograms, with a mossy yellow-green husk that typically cracks slightly at the base when ripe, enclosing thick, deep-yellow, dry (non-sticky) flesh with a rich, buttery sweetness, and a comparatively high share of flat, underdeveloped seeds that boosts the edible-flesh ratio compared to older regional selections. It has become the dominant durian cultivar in Mekong Delta orchards, valued by growers for reliable yields and relative ease of cultivation. Grow it exactly as other grafted durian: deep, fertile, well-drained soil, consistent warmth and humidity, and shelter from wind, easing irrigation slightly as fruit nears maturity to concentrate sugar and aroma.

common_name: Xoài Cát Chu Mango (Cát Chu Mango)

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun in well-drained soil, or grow in a large container in marginal climates so it can be sheltered from any frost.

directions: Cát Chu takes its name from Cao Lãnh district in Đồng Tháp province, in Vietnam's Mekong Delta, where it is grown alongside the larger Cát Hòa Lộc as one of the region's two signature dessert mangoes. The fruit is noticeably smaller than Cát Hòa Lộc, rounded at the shoulder and tapering toward the tip, typically weighing around 250 to 350 grams, with thin skin that ripens from green to golden yellow over a small, flat seed surrounded by nearly fiberless, soft orange-yellow flesh carrying a mild, distinctive fragrance and balanced sweetness. Mature trees are highly productive and the cultivar is propagated almost exclusively by grafting or budding onto seedling rootstock rather than grown from seed. Grow it as other mango: full sun, deep well-drained soil, and a pronounced dry spell before flowering, with frost protection or container culture required outside the warmest subtropical and tropical zones.
sources: Southern Horticultural Research Institute (SOFRI), Vietnam

common_name: Thanh Hà Lychee (Vải Thiều Thanh Hà)

planting.note: Plant only where winters stay above freezing; young trees are frost-sensitive and benefit from wind protection and a brief cool, dry spell before bloom.

directions: Thanh Hà lychee traces back to a single tree planted around 1870 in Thanh Hà district, Hải Dương province, by a fruit trader named Hoàng Văn Côm, who is said to have brought the stock home after tasting an exceptional lychee at a gathering of the Chinese community in Hải Phòng. That original 'ancestral tree,' still alive and fruiting, was formally recognized by the Vietnam Gardening Association in 1992, and scions taken from it spread the variety first through Hải Dương and later into Bắc Giang, Quảng Ninh, and parts of southern Vietnam. Grown in the fertile alluvial soils along the Thái Bình River, it produces notably large, sweet, fragrant fruit considered superior to the parent stock from which it descended. Propagate by grafting onto seedling rootstock, grow in full sun with a brief cool, relatively dry period before bloom, and protect young trees from wind, frost, and waterlogged soil.
